source_refs.note: Chapter 19 exercise (PDF 150-154), solved: 19 MCQs (16-34) keyed from the chapter's text, 8 short (Q24's 17 pairs separately), 17 long and 6 inquisitive questions with model answers. No answer key is printed. Book corrections: MCQ 31, 32, Short Q24, Long Q29-30, Inq Q12.

blocks.prompt: 16. Which of the following looks like beads on a string?
blocks.explanation: About 146 nucleotides of DNA wrap twice around each histone octamer to form nucleosomes, joined by linker DNA; the chain of nucleosomes resembles beads on a string, the nucleosome string (11 nm) (19.1.2).

blocks.prompt: 17. The most convincing proof that DNA is the genetic material was provided by;
blocks.explanation: Hershey and Chase (1952) showed that 32P-labelled phage DNA entered the bacteria and directed new phages, while the 35S-labelled protein coat stayed outside (19.2.2). Meselson and Stahl proved semi-conservative replication, not that DNA is the genetic material.

blocks.prompt: 18. Degeneracy of genetic code means that;

options.text: Multiple codons can specify the same amino acid
Same codon can specify multiple amino acids
Each codon is read independently of the adjacent codons

blocks.explanation: Degeneracy means that multiple codons can specify the same amino acid (19.4.2). Option (a) describes the triplet nature and (d) the non-overlapping nature of the code.

blocks.prompt: 19. How many codons are needed to specify for five amino acids?
blocks.explanation: Each codon (three nucleotides) specifies one amino acid, so five amino acids need five codons (15 nucleotides) (19.4.1).

blocks.prompt: 20. Which of the following is NOT involved in the initiation of replication?
blocks.explanation: Helicase, gyrase, single-strand binding proteins and primase act while the helix is opened and the primer is built; DNA ligase works at the end, joining the Okazaki fragments (19.3.3).

blocks.prompt: 21. Why DNA polymerase synthesises the leading and lagging strands of DNA in different manners?

options.text: The origins of replication occur only at the 5′ end
DNA ligase works only in the 3′ to 5′ direction
DNA polymerase can only work on one strand at a time
DNA polymerase can join new nucleotides only to the 3′ end of strand

blocks.explanation: DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides only to the 3′ end, so it builds in the 5′ to 3′ direction. As the two template strands are antiparallel, one strand is made continuously (leading) and the other in Okazaki fragments (lagging) (19.3.3).

blocks.prompt: 22. Synthesis of a new DNA strand usually begins with:
blocks.explanation: Primase lays down a short RNA primer (5-10 RNA nucleotides); DNA polymerase III adds the first DNA nucleotide to its 3′ end (19.3.3).

blocks.prompt: 23. The elongation of the leading strand during DNA synthesis;

options.text: Progresses away from the replication fork
Depends on the action of polymerase

blocks.explanation: The leading strand is extended continuously by DNA polymerase III, towards the fork and in the 5′ to 3′ direction; Okazaki fragments and growth away from the fork belong to the lagging strand (19.3.3).

blocks.prompt: 24. Which of the following enzymes remove supercoiling in replicating DNA ahead of the replication fork?
blocks.explanation: Unwinding produces supercoils ahead of the fork; gyrase (a topoisomerase) attaches ahead of the fork and removes them (19.3.3). Helicases unwind the helix itself.

blocks.prompt: 25. Which enzyme joins the bits of DNA?
blocks.explanation: DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds (19.3.3); it is also the 'molecular glue' of genetic engineering.

blocks.prompt: 26. Which of these subunits of RNA polymerase is required to initiate transcription?
blocks.explanation: The σ subunit recognises the promoter and initiates synthesis; after binding it is removed and the core enzyme continues (19.5).

blocks.prompt: 27. When and where does the splicing of mRNA occur?
blocks.explanation: Splicing is a post-transcriptional modification of the new eukaryotic mRNA before it leaves the nucleus for the cytoplasm (19.5).

blocks.prompt: 28. What happens in mRNA splicing?

options.text: Introns and exons are removed from the gene
Introns and exons are joined together
Exons are removed and introns are joined together
Introns are removed and exons are joined together

blocks.explanation: Introns (non-coding regions) are removed from the immature mRNA and the remaining exons are joined, so the mature mRNA carries the coding sequence only (19.5).

blocks.prompt: 29. Which of these happens first during protein synthesis?

options.text: Binding of aminoacyl t-RNA with ribosome
Binding of release factor with ribosome

blocks.explanation: In initiation, the first aminoacyl-tRNA binds to the smaller ribosomal subunit. Peptide bond formation and translocation come in elongation, and the release factor acts at termination (19.6).

blocks.prompt: 30. The synthesis of protein chains is initiated with the amino acid;
blocks.explanation: The start codon AUG specifies methionine; in prokaryotes it is the modified N-formyl methionine (19.4.1, 19.6).

blocks.prompt: 31. The main function of tRNA is to:

options.text: Bind the mRNA with the smaller ribosomal subunit
Bind the complementary RNA and DNA strands together
bring amino acids from the cytoplasm to the ribosomes?

blocks.explanation: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid (as aminoacyl-tRNA) to the ribosome and places it by matching its anticodon with the mRNA codon (19.6).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (d) is printed beginning with a small letter and ending with a stray question mark: "bring amino acids from the cytoplasm to the ribosomes?". It should read "Bring amino acids from the cytoplasm to the ribosomes".

blocks.prompt: 32. Ultraviolet radiation can cause mutations by;

options.text: Making double covalent bonds between adjacent pyrimidine bases
Breaking phosphodiester bonds in DNA strands

blocks.explanation: When two adjacent pyrimidine nucleotides (C and T) absorb UV, a double covalent bond forms between them, which can block replication. Breaking phosphodiester bonds is the effect of ionizing radiation (X rays, gamma rays) (19.8.1).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) is printed "Adding nucleotides in NA"; "NA" is a misprint for "DNA" (Adding nucleotides in DNA).

blocks.prompt: 33. Phenylketonuria is a genetic disorder with a defect in the metabolism of:
blocks.explanation: In PKU the liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is not made properly, so the amino acid phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine and builds up (19.8.1).

blocks.prompt: 34. The condition sickle cell anaemia is due to;
blocks.explanation: In the β-globin gene the DNA nucleotide T is substituted by A, so CTC (glutamic acid) becomes CAC (valine): a substitution point mutation (19.8.1).

blocks.prompt: 17. What are the four types of chromosomes on the basis of position of centromere?
blocks.explanation:
1. Metacentric: centromere at the centre (two equal arms).
2. Sub-metacentric: centromere slightly away from the centre.
3. Acrocentric: centromere near one end.
4. Telocentric: centromere at the end.

blocks.prompt: 18. What is chromatin fibre? How is it formed during condensation of chromatin?
blocks.explanation:
Chromatin fibre is the 30 nm thick fibre of tightly packed nucleosomes.
Formation: DNA wraps around histone octamers to form the nucleosome string (11 nm); in the early stages of cell division this string coils again about its axis, and the condensed nucleosomes make the thicker 30 nm chromatin fibre, which later folds into a 300 nm supercoil.

blocks.prompt: 19. Briefly describe the concept of gene and gene locus.
blocks.explanation:
Gene: the basic unit of heredity (term by Johannsen, 1909); a short segment of DNA that encodes the sequence of amino acids of a particular polypeptide.
Gene locus: the specific location of a gene on a chromosome (plural loci); alleles of a gene lie at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

blocks.prompt: 20. State the functions of DNA polymerase I, II and III.
blocks.explanation:
DNA polymerase I: removes the RNA primers and fills the gaps (including those between Okazaki fragments) with DNA nucleotides.
DNA polymerase II: repairs DNA damage during the life of the cell.
DNA polymerase III: the main replicating enzyme; adds nucleotides to the 3′ end in the 5′ to 3′ direction to build leading and lagging strands, and proofreads.

blocks.prompt: 21. State the central dogma of gene expression.
blocks.explanation: Central dogma (Francis Crick): genetic information flows from DNA to an RNA copy of the gene, and the RNA directs the assembly of amino acids into a protein: DNA → RNA → Protein. It has two steps, transcription and translation; the flow is one-way and information in a protein never goes back.

blocks.prompt: 22. What do you mean by “degeneracy of genetic code”?
blocks.explanation: Degeneracy means that more than one codon can specify the same amino acid (64 codons code for only 20 amino acids), e.g. GGC and GGU both code for glycine. It makes the code tolerant of some mutations (silent mutations) and gives evolutionary flexibility.

blocks.prompt: 23. Enlist some commonly occurring minor mutations in human.
blocks.explanation:
1. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs): one-nucleotide changes, e.g. inability to digest lactose.
2. Insertions and deletions: e.g. a three-nucleotide deletion in cystic fibrosis.
3. Silent mutations: no change in amino acid (GGC to GGU, both glycine).
4. Missense mutations: one amino acid changed, e.g. sickle cell anaemia.
5. Nonsense mutations: premature stop codon, e.g. Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

rows: Protein is made using the information in mRNA

blocks.explanation: The genetic code is the whole message; a codon is one 'word' of it.

One unit of the genetic code

blocks.prompt: 15. Annotate the detailed structure of a chromosome.
blocks.explanation:
Morphology (a duplicated, condensed chromosome; labelled diagram in words):
1. Two sister chromatids: identical strands formed after replication in interphase.
2. Centromere: the constriction joining the chromatids; a specific DNA sequence of about 220 nucleotides.
3. Kinetochore: disc-shaped protein structure on the centromere, where spindle fibres attach.
4. Secondary constriction (nucleolar organizer region, NOR): makes the nucleolus in interphase.
5. Satellite: knob-like end beyond the secondary constriction, with highly repetitive (junk) DNA.
6. Telomeres: terminal ends that stop chromosomes sticking to each other end to end.
Types by centromere position: metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric.
Chemical composition and organisation:
1. About 40% DNA and 60% proteins (histones). DNA is negatively charged (phosphate); histones are positively charged (arginine, lysine), so they bind strongly.
2. Nucleosome string (11 nm): about 146 nucleotides of DNA wrap twice around an octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4); nucleosomes are joined by about 80 nucleotides of linker DNA; histone H1 sits at the entry and exit points.
3. Chromatin fibre (30 nm): the nucleosome string coils again.
4. Supercoil (300 nm): the fibre folds on itself.
5. Chromatid (700 nm): the supercoil coils and condenses further.

blocks.prompt: 16. Explain the concept of alleles as the alternative forms of a gene.
blocks.explanation:
1. A gene is a short segment of DNA that codes for a particular polypeptide and so controls a character; its location on a chromosome is its locus.
2. Body cells of diploid organisms have chromosomes in homologous pairs, one from each parent.
3. The alternate forms of a gene are alleles. They are present at the same locus on the two homologous chromosomes. If one chromosome carries an allele for eye colour at a locus, its homologue carries an allele for eye colour at the same locus.
4. Alleles differ slightly in their nucleotide sequence, so they code for slightly different products and give different forms of the same character (e.g. different eye colours).
5. New alleles arise by mutation; a person has two alleles of each gene, which may be the same or different.

blocks.prompt: 17. Narrate the experimental work of Griffith that proved that DNA is the hereditary material.
blocks.explanation:
Griffith (1928) worked on Streptococcus pneumoniae, which has two strains:
- S-type: polysaccharide coat, smooth colonies, virulent.
- R-type: no coat, rough colonies, non-virulent.
Experiments on mice:
1. Live S-type injected: mice got pneumonia and died.
2. Live R-type injected: mice lived.
3. Heat-killed S-type injected: mice lived.
4. Heat-killed S-type + live R-type injected: mice died, and live S-type bacteria were found in their blood.
Conclusion: some material passed from the dead S-type to the live R-type and gave it the information to make a coat and become virulent. He called this transformation (transfer of genetic material from one organism to another, changing the recipient's genetic makeup). Griffith could not tell whether this material was DNA, protein or both.
Later, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) removed proteins from dead S-type: transformation still occurred; removing DNA stopped it. So DNA is the transforming principle, the hereditary material.

blocks.prompt: 18. Narrate the experimental work of Hershey and Chase that proved that DNA is the hereditary material.
blocks.explanation:
Hershey and Chase (1952) used a bacteriophage (DNA core and protein coat) that injects material into a bacterium, which then makes new phages.
Question: does the phage inject DNA, protein or both?
Labelling:
1. Phages grown on 35S: sulphur goes into amino acids, so the protein coat is labelled (DNA has no sulphur).
2. Phages grown on 32P: phosphorus goes into phosphate groups, so the DNA is labelled (protein has little phosphorus).
Setups: setup 1, 35S-protein phages infect bacteria; setup 2, 32P-DNA phages infect bacteria. After some time the bacterial cells and the medium were separated by centrifugation and checked for radioactivity.
Results:
- Setup 1: radioactivity in the medium, not in the bacteria.
- Setup 2: radioactivity in the bacteria, not in the medium.
Conclusion: the phage DNA entered the bacteria and directed the making of new phages, while the protein coat stayed outside. So DNA, not protein, is the hereditary material.

blocks.prompt: 19. Describe the three models proposed about the mechanism of DNA replication.
blocks.explanation:
1. Conservative model: the parent double helix remains intact and acts as a pattern for a wholly new double helix. After replication, one daughter DNA has both parent strands and the other has both new strands.
2. Semi-conservative model: the two parent strands separate and each acts as a template for a new strand. Each daughter DNA has one parent strand and one new strand.
3. Dispersive model: the parent DNA breaks and disperses into nucleotides, which combine with new nucleotides; all four strands of the daughter DNAs are mixtures of old and new pieces.
Meselson and Stahl (1958) showed that DNA replicates by the semi-conservative model.

rows: One all-old double helix, one all-new
Both hybrid: one old strand + one new strand
Both have strands that are mixtures of old and new

blocks.prompt: 20. Narrate the work of Meselson and Stahl to justify the semi-conservative replication.
blocks.explanation:
Experiment (1958):
1. E. coli bacteria were grown for many generations on a medium with heavy nitrogen 15N, so their DNA became dense (15N-DNA).
2. They were moved to a medium with normal 14N, and DNA samples were collected at intervals.
3. DNA was dissolved in caesium chloride solution and ultracentrifuged; a density gradient formed and each DNA settled where its density matched the caesium (heavy DNA lower, light DNA higher).
Observations and explanation:
- 0 minutes (no replication): one heavy band; both strands 15N.
- 20 minutes (first replication): one intermediate band; every DNA was a hybrid of one 15N and one 14N strand.
- 40 minutes (second replication): two bands, one intermediate and one light; each hybrid gave a heavy strand to a new hybrid and a light strand to an all-14N DNA.
Conclusion: each daughter DNA keeps one parent strand and makes one new strand, so replication is semi-conservative. (The conservative model would have given heavy and light bands after the first replication; the dispersive model would never give a separate light band.)

blocks.prompt: 21. Describe the events of the process of DNA replication.
blocks.explanation:
Replication occurs in the S-phase; steps (as in prokaryotes):
1. Opening the double helix: an initiator protein binds the replication origin (one in prokaryotes, many in eukaryotes). Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, forming two Y-shaped replication forks (a replication bubble). Gyrase (topoisomerase) ahead of the fork removes supercoils. Single-strand binding proteins keep the strands apart. The forks move away from each other.
2. Building a primer: primase lays a short RNA primer (5-10 RNA nucleotides) on each template at the origin.
3. Extension: DNA polymerase III adds deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP) by base pairing (A-T, C-G); removal of two phosphates gives the energy. It adds only to the 3′ end, so it builds 5′ to 3′.
- Leading strand: made continuously towards the fork from one primer.
- Lagging strand: made discontinuously away from the fork as Okazaki fragments, each with its own primer.
4. Termination: at the termination site (origin to termination site = replicon), DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers and fills the gaps with DNA, and DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments.
Polymerase III also proofreads, giving stability; rare uncorrected errors are mutations, giving variability.

blocks.prompt: 22. Explain the mechanism of transcription.
blocks.explanation:
Transcription is the synthesis of RNA complementary to the template (antisense) strand of DNA; the other strand is the coding (sense) strand. No primer is needed.
1. Initiation: RNA polymerase binds the promoter (not itself transcribed): in prokaryotes TTGACA (-35 sequence) and TATAAT (-10 sequence); in eukaryotes the TATA box TATAAA (-25) and CAAT box GGCCAATCT (-70). RNA polymerase has five subunits: two α (bind regulatory proteins), β′ (binds template DNA), β (binds RNA nucleotides) and σ (recognises the promoter and initiates). After binding, σ leaves; the core enzyme unwinds DNA and forms the transcription bubble.
2. Elongation: RNA polymerase joins ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) complementary to the template in the 5′ to 3′ direction, usually starting with A or G; two phosphates are released as energy. The first 12 bases make a temporary RNA-DNA helix that keeps the 3′ end at the catalytic site. The bubble moves along the DNA, the mRNA protrudes, and the DNA rewinds behind.
3. Termination: after the gene's stop sequence there is a GC-rich region followed by AT pairs. The transcribed GC region pairs within the RNA to form a GC hairpin, followed by a tail of four or more U. The hairpin makes the polymerase pause; the weak U-A pairs cannot hold the hybrid, so the RNA separates and transcription stops.
In eukaryotes the new mRNA then gets a 5′ cap and poly-A tail and is spliced.

blocks.prompt: 23. Describe the mechanism of protein synthesis.
blocks.explanation:
Translation uses the mRNA message to join amino acids into a polypeptide.
Activation of amino acids: aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (20 kinds) attaches each amino acid to its specific tRNA, forming aminoacyl-tRNA (aa-tRNA).
1. Initiation: the first aa-tRNA (N-formyl methionine in prokaryotes, methionine in eukaryotes) binds the small ribosomal subunit with an initiation factor; another initiation factor binds the 5′ end of mRNA and places the anticodon over the start codon AUG; the large subunit joins. The ribosome has a P site (peptide bond), A site (incoming aa-tRNA) and E site (exit), arranged E-P-A from 5′ to 3′.
2. Elongation: (i) the next aa-tRNA binds the A site with the elongation factor; (ii) peptidyl transferase moves the amino acid (chain) from the tRNA at P and joins it by a peptide bond to the amino acid at A; (iii) the ribosome moves three nucleotides towards 3′ (translocation); the tRNA with the chain shifts from A to P, the empty tRNA goes to E and leaves, and a new codon is exposed at A; (iv) repeated until a stop codon reaches A.
3. Termination: no tRNA matches the stop codon; a release factor recognises it and frees the polypeptide; the tRNA leaves and the ribosomal subunits separate from the mRNA.

blocks.prompt: 24. Describe the difference between protein synthesis in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
blocks.explanation: The mechanism is the same in both, but the following points differ.

rows: mRNA translated immediately; no post-transcriptional modification
mRNA modified first: introns cut out, 5′ cap and 3′ poly-A tail added
Transcription and translation both in cytoplasm
Transcription in nucleus; translation in cytoplasm and on RER

blocks.prompt: 25. Describe the importance of the regulation of gene expression.
blocks.explanation:
Not all genes work at the same time or in every cell; switching genes ON and OFF and controlling their timing by regulator proteins is regulation of gene expression.
Importance:
1. Cells respond to changes in the environment and make a protein only when it is needed, saving energy and materials.
2. In multicellular organisms it is the basis of cell differentiation and morphogenesis: all cells have the same genome, but different genes are expressed in different cell types, creating different cell types. E.g. liver cells express the alcohol dehydrogenase genes, while brain neurons keep them OFF.
3. Different genes are expressed at different times of development.
4. Alternative splicing lets one gene give more than one polypeptide in different cells.
Levels: transcription (rate of transcription), post-transcription (mRNA modification), translation (rate of translation) and post-translation (protein folding, stability).

blocks.prompt: 26. Describe the negative and positive control of gene expression.
blocks.explanation:
At the transcription level, genes have regulatory sequences to which specific regulatory proteins bind.
1. Negative control: regulatory proteins called repressors bind to operators (DNA pieces near the promoter). The bound repressor blocks RNA polymerase, so transcription stops or is reduced; the gene is OFF.
2. Positive control: regulatory proteins called activators (inducers) bind to the operators and help RNA polymerase bind the promoter, so transcription starts or speeds up; the gene is ON.
Also, in eukaryotes, regulatory proteins in particular cell types control splicing, removing introns or exons in different ways, so one gene gives different mRNAs and polypeptides.

rows: Repressor binds operator and blocks RNA polymerase
Activator helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter

blocks.prompt: 27. Explain the post-transcriptional modification of mRNA.
blocks.explanation:
In prokaryotes the mRNA is translated at once in the cytoplasm. In eukaryotes the new (immature) mRNA must travel from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, so it is modified:
1. 5′ cap: a methylated GTP is joined to the first nucleotide (A or G) by a 5′-5′ linkage; it protects the mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases.
2. 3′ poly-A tail: about 250 A nucleotides are added at the 3′ end; it protects the transcript from degradation by nucleases.
3. Splicing: introns (non-coding regions) are removed and exons are joined, so the mature mRNA has only coding segments. Because introns are cut out, the mature mRNA that reaches the cytoplasm is shorter than the original transcript.
Alternative splicing in different cells can give different polypeptides from one gene.

blocks.prompt: 28. Write a note on point mutations and their sources.
blocks.explanation:
Point mutations change one or a few nucleotides (the most common gene mutations).
Types:
1. Substitution: one nucleotide replaced by another (e.g. A by G); sickle cell anaemia.
2. Insertion: one or more extra nucleotides added, usually by replication errors.
3. Deletion: one or more nucleotides removed; e.g. a three-nucleotide deletion in cystic fibrosis.
Effects: silent (same amino acid), missense (one amino acid changed), nonsense (premature stop codon).
Sources:
1. Physical damage: ionizing radiation (X rays, gamma rays) makes free radicals that break phosphodiester bonds; UV light makes double covalent bonds between adjacent pyrimidines (C, T), blocking replication.
2. Mutagen chemicals: some resemble nucleotides and get into DNA; some remove amino groups from adenine or cytosine or add hydrocarbon groups, causing mispairing (e.g. mustard gas).
3. Spontaneous: nucleotides shift to alternative forms and mispair during replication; misaligned homologous chromosomes form loops that are cut out, deleting hundreds of nucleotides.

blocks.prompt: 29. Describe the symptoms, causes and treatments Down syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome.
blocks.explanation:
Down syndrome
Cause: non-disjunction of autosome pair 21, usually during egg formation; an egg with 24 chromosomes fertilised by a normal sperm gives trisomy 21 (2n+1 = 47), male or female. About 1 in 750 children; risk rises with the mother's age.
Symptoms: mental impairment, stunted growth, extra skin on back and neck, flat face, small head, short neck and limbs, upward slanting eyes, small ears, poor muscles, protruding tongue, heart defects; males usually sterile, females less fertile.
Treatment (management): screening for common problems, medical treatment where needed, good family environment, special education and proper care.
Klinefelter syndrome
Cause: non-disjunction of sex chromosomes; an XX egg fertilised by a Y sperm, or an XY sperm fertilising an X egg, gives 44+XXY = 47 (described by Harry Klinefelter, 1942).
Symptoms: sterile male with female characters (less body hair, breast growth), small testes, long legs, short trunk, shoulders equal to hips, less deep voice.
Treatment: testosterone at puberty, surgical removal of breast tissue, behavioural therapy for language, school and social problems.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Long questions 29 and 30 are printed without "of": "causes and treatments Down syndrome" and "causes and treatments Turner syndrome". They mean "treatments of Down syndrome" and "treatments of Turner syndrome"; the next question (31) prints "of".

blocks.prompt: 30. Describe the symptoms, causes and treatments Turner syndrome.
blocks.explanation:
Cause: non-disjunction of sex chromosomes produces an egg (or sperm) with no sex chromosome (O). If an O egg is fertilised by an X sperm (or an O sperm fertilises an X egg), the zygote is 44+XO = 45 (2n-1), monosomy of the sex chromosomes; it develops into a sterile female (described by Henry Turner, 1938). (An OY zygote cannot survive, as genes of the X chromosome are essential.) About 1 in 5000 female births.
Symptoms: short stature, webbed neck, immature sex organs and infertility, low mental abilities, small chin and jaw; also liver and kidney problems, obesity, diabetes and hypertension.
Treatment: growth hormone started early in childhood helps reach adult height; estrogen replacement therapy develops the secondary sexual characters.

blocks.prompt: 31. Describe the symptoms, causes and treatments of Sickle cell anaemia and phenylketonuria.
blocks.explanation:
Sickle cell anaemia
Cause: a recessive allele of the β-globin gene of haemoglobin (chromosome 11) with a substitution point mutation: DNA T replaced by A, so CTC (glutamic acid) becomes CAC (valine). A child with two mutant alleles makes abnormal β chains; the haemoglobin carries less oxygen and the RBCs become sickle-shaped.
Symptoms: pain, fatigue, shortness of breath, jaundice, increased risk of infections.
Treatment: pain relief (NSAIDs, opioids), blood transfusions to add healthy RBCs, bone marrow transplant (long-term cure), regular monitoring, vaccinations and antibiotics.
Phenylketonuria (PKU)
Cause: a normal gene on chromosome 12 makes the liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts phenylalanine into tyrosine. A point mutation (substitution or deletion) makes a recessive allele; with two recessive alleles PAH is not made properly and phenylalanine builds up to toxic levels.
Symptoms: intellectual disability, seizures, behavioural problems, mental disorder, microcephaly, musty odour of breath, skin and urine; brain damage.
Treatment: diet low in phenylalanine (avoid meat, dairy, eggs, some grains), regular blood phenylalanine monitoring, medicines with synthetic PAH, vitamin and mineral supplements.

blocks.prompt: 7. DNA is tightly wrapped around histone proteins. How can replication enzymes read the code if it is buried inside a coil?
blocks.explanation: Replication does not happen while DNA is condensed into a chromosome. It happens in the S-phase of interphase, when the chromatin is uncoiled into a fine network. At replication origins the nucleosome packing is loosened (beyond the chapter: chromatin-remodelling proteins and histone modifications loosen or slide the nucleosomes), so the DNA becomes accessible. Then helicase unwinds the helix, gyrase removes supercoils and single-strand binding proteins keep the strands open, so the polymerase can read the bases. Behind the fork the DNA is packed again with old and newly made histones (new histones are made during chromatin duplication).

blocks.prompt: 8. Our genetic code uses three-letter "words" to create 20 amino acids. Could a complex human exist if the code used only two-letter words?
blocks.explanation: No. With four nucleotides, two-letter codons give only 4 x 4 = 16 combinations, fewer than the 20 amino acids, and none would be left for start and stop signals. At most 16 kinds of amino acid could be coded, so many human proteins (enzymes, haemoglobin, antibodies) could not be made with their correct sequences, and a complex human could not exist. A triplet code gives 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 codons, more than enough for 20 amino acids plus start and stop codons; the extra codons also give degeneracy, which protects against some mutations.

blocks.prompt: 9. DNA Polymerase III is a highly efficient proof-reader that fixes its own mistakes. What happens to a cell if the gene for the "proof-reader" enzyme itself gets a mutation?
blocks.explanation: The enzyme made from the mutated gene would proofread poorly or not at all. Then mispaired nucleotides made during replication would not be corrected, so the error rate of every replication would rise. DNA would lose its stability: mutations would accumulate in all genes with each division, including genes that control growth and division, and errors would multiply further (beyond the chapter: such cells are called 'mutator' cells). Results: faulty or non-functional proteins, cell death, or uncontrolled division leading to cancer (mutations disrupting gene regulation can contribute to cancer). If it happens in germ cells, the defects pass to offspring.

blocks.prompt: 10. Why the length of transcribed mRNA molecule (in eukaryotes) shortens as it enters the cytoplasm for translation?
blocks.explanation: Because of splicing. Eukaryotic genes contain introns (non-coding regions) between exons, and the whole gene is transcribed into an immature mRNA. Before the mRNA leaves the nucleus, the introns are cut out and the exons are joined, so the mature mRNA that reaches the cytoplasm contains only coding segments and is shorter than the original transcript (even though a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail are added). Prokaryotic genes have no introns, so their mRNA is not shortened.

blocks.prompt: 11. How many types of tRNA molecules are necessary for a living cell, if the genetic code is a triplet code?
blocks.explanation: A triplet code has 64 codons; 3 are stop codons with no anticodon, leaving 61 sense codons. If each sense codon needed its own tRNA with a complementary anticodon, the cell would need 61 types of tRNA. At the very least 20 types are needed, one for each amino acid, since each amino acid has its own aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and tRNA. (Beyond the chapter: because of 'wobble', the third base of a codon can pair loosely, so one tRNA can read more than one codon; cells therefore manage with fewer than 61 kinds, but more than 20.)

blocks.prompt: 12. After isotopic labelling of the starting DNA with15N, Meselson and Stahl continue their experiment to at least two rounds of replication instead of stopping the experiment after only one round of replication. Justify their decision to continue to at least two replications.
blocks.explanation:
After one replication they saw a single intermediate (hybrid) band. This ruled out the conservative model (which would give one heavy and one light band), but it fitted both the semi-conservative and the dispersive models, since in both every daughter DNA would be half 15N and half 14N.
The second replication separates these two:
- Semi-conservative: each hybrid gives one hybrid and one all-14N DNA, so two bands, intermediate and light.
- Dispersive: every DNA would be a mixture of about one-quarter 15N, giving a single band between intermediate and light, never a separate light band.
They observed two bands (intermediate and light), so only the semi-conservative model fits. Hence at least two rounds were needed to decide.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question is printed "with15N" with no space; it should read "with 15N" (heavy nitrogen, nitrogen-15).
